title: Work Bus

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Is this like a blooper reel?' Andy: 'A blooper reel? What is this, 2005? Do I look like Bob Saget?'
jokes.setup: Oscar reasonably describes what the video actually is
jokes.punchline: Andy indignantly rejects the accurate description with a dated pop culture reference, unaware his 'fail' concept is equally passé
jokes.explanation: The irony is layered and well-executed: Andy dismisses 'blooper reels' as 2005-era content while his 'FAIL!' concept is itself already passé by 2012. The Bob Saget reference lands because it's specific and Andy delivering it with total sincerity is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Clark to camera: 'And I'm Clark, I like to eat toilet paper. We fail!'
jokes.setup: Following Pete's self-introduction, Clark does his own
jokes.punchline: The random, inexplicable 'I like to eat toilet paper' non sequitur as his defining trait
jokes.explanation: Random absurdism with no real grounding in character. Works as a quick throwaway but 'I eat toilet paper' is a cheap randomness joke rather than earned character comedy. Functional but lazy.

jokes.text: Andy solemnly pauses the fail reel to memorialize Jerry from the warehouse who 'passed away this year,' then immediately cuts back to 'Well, that's all, folks!'
jokes.setup: The fail reel has a brief solemn in memoriam moment for a deceased warehouse worker
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately follows the death tribute with 'Well, that's all, folks! Ski you later, everybody!'
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely dark and effective. Andy's obliviousness reaches its peak here — including a death notice in a fail video and then pivot immediately to a chirpy sign-off is a perfectly constructed cringe moment. 'Ski you later' makes it worse in the best way. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'That was just normal video with you making vulgar noises.' Andy: 'Well, I worked with what I had, Oscar.'
jokes.setup: Oscar accurately critiques that Andy's fail reel was just footage with fake sound effects
jokes.punchline: Andy's unabashed, defensive non-answer: 'I worked with what I had'
jokes.explanation: Oscar plays perfect straight man and Andy's defense is delivered with such earnest conviction that it lands. 'I worked with what I had' is the kind of deflection that reveals character — Andy genuinely doesn't understand why this is a problem.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'That was not a fail!' Group responds: 'Fail! Fail! Fail!' Dwight: 'That was actually a serious accident that could have resulted in severe bodily harm.' Group: 'Fail! Fail! Fail! You're all failing right now. Congratulations on your epic fail of the use of the word fail!'
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Dwight) appears to have a serious accident in Jim's video
jokes.punchline: Dwight's humorless, lawyerly protest against the use of 'fail' for a genuine accident, while the crowd just chants 'Fail!' at his protests
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dwight — he can't let the semantic imprecision go. 'Congratulations on your epic fail of the use of the word fail' is a great line that only Dwight would deliver with complete seriousness. The group chanting 'Fail!' at his protests escalates the joke beautifully.

jokes.text: The landlord is measuring the office with an EMF detector and Dwight says 'It's a beehive in the wall?'
jokes.setup: The landlord is measuring electromagnetic fields in the office with a detector
jokes.punchline: Dwight's first instinct is that it must be detecting a beehive
jokes.explanation: Very Dwight — his preoccupation with bees is well-established. The landlord's incredulous response ('You think I have a machine for measuring beehives?') is the real kicker. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: Landlord to Toby: 'How are you not murdered every hour?'
jokes.setup: Toby has presumably said something pedantic or annoying about the EMF readings
jokes.punchline: The landlord's exasperated rhetorical question perfectly captures everyone's barely-suppressed rage at Toby
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical line that captures the universal Office sentiment about Toby in six words. The fact that it comes from an outsider (the landlord) who has just met Toby makes it even funnier — it's immediately obvious to anyone. High quotability.

jokes.text: Landlord: 'Oh, the wires need insulation. It's a wire, people. I'm not buying it a fur coat.'
jokes.setup: The landlord is dismissing the EMF concerns by minimizing the need for wire insulation
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not buying it a fur coat' — an absurdly specific and funny metaphor for insulation
jokes.explanation: Sharp, original line with a vivid specific image. 'Fur coat' for insulation is a genuinely clever metaphor that's unexpected. The landlord's mercenary attitude is well-established in a single line. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jim confessional: He describes wanting to do 'something huge' for Pam, then compares it to protecting her from bikers in a biker bar — complete with dramatized 'Wham! You've got to go through me first!'
jokes.setup: Jim wants to do something big for Pam after she was cool about his Philly job
jokes.punchline: His fantasy scenario escalates to an absurdly specific biker bar protection fantasy, complete with sound effects
jokes.explanation: Jim's confessionals are usually understated, so this shift into dramatic fantasy mode is funny. The specificity of 'some bikers' and the self-aggrandizing 'Wham!' is characteristically dorky Jim trying to be heroic. The joke is that his romantic gesture impulse produces this ridiculous scenario.

jokes.text: Andy produces a literal hourglass when Dwight asks for a minute of his time, narrating every grain of sand with baroque language
jokes.setup: Dwight asks for 'a word' and Andy says he'll give him one minute
jokes.punchline: Andy pulls out an actual hourglass and delivers an increasingly elaborate monologue about the passing time, eating up the very minute he's supposedly giving
jokes.explanation: Genuinely inventive bit. The hourglass itself is funny, but Andy narrating 'no time will be added at the end, even to accommodate this sentence, with all of its baroque dependent clauses and cascading turns of phrase' is self-aware wordplay that only this version of Andy could deliver. The meta quality of describing his own verbose speech while being verbose lands. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I'm trying to adopt a baby.' Andy: 'A baby what?' Dwight: 'A human?'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces he's trying to adopt a baby
jokes.punchline: Andy's genuine confusion about the species, Dwight's incredulous clarification
jokes.explanation: Three words — 'A baby what?' — capture everything about Andy's particular brand of dim obliviousness. Dwight's incredulous 'A human?' is the ideal straight-man response. Very economical, very well-structured. The brevity is the joke's greatest asset.

jokes.text: Andy accuses Dwight of running a 'plagiarism entrapment scheme' by asking him to sign a letter Dwight wrote himself
jokes.setup: Dwight explains he'd write the character reference letter himself and just need Andy to sign it
jokes.punchline: Andy refuses, citing 'plagiarism entrapment' — a completely nonsensical legal theory delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: 'Plagiarism entrapment scheme' is a brilliant piece of nonsense legalese that Andy delivers with total conviction. Only Andy would invent this concept and believe it. The joke works because the words almost make sense — 'entrapment' is vaguely legal, 'plagiarism' is sort of relevant — but combined they're pure absurdist Andy logic.

jokes.text: Andy narrates the hourglass during Dwight's pitch: '...and those sand grains are tumbling with fury down the side of the hourglass.' Time's up mid-sentence.
jokes.setup: Andy set a one-minute timer on the hourglass and promised no extensions
jokes.punchline: He keeps narrating the hourglass, cutting Dwight off mid-argument, and rigidly calls time
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the hourglass bit. The comedy is in Andy's literal enforcement and Dwight/Andy talking over each other. Dwight finally making his actual point in the last seconds while Andy narrates sand is funny layered chaos.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Sure, I'll read her letter. And if she tells the truth about how evil and unfit to be a mother she is, then yeah, I'll sign that.'
jokes.setup: Andy grudgingly agrees to read Nellie's adoption character reference letter
jokes.punchline: His 'agreement' is actually a trap — he'll only sign it if it's an honest condemnation of Nellie
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke — Andy's grudge against Nellie is well-established and his passive-aggressive 'generosity' here is in character. Works as exposition delivery but isn't particularly clever construction.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'I already ditched my uterus, and I ain't losing any more good parts!'
jokes.setup: The landlord says fixing the wiring would require shutting the office down for a week
jokes.punchline: Meredith reacts to the EMF health concerns with this announcement about her hysterectomy
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Meredith line. 'I already ditched my uterus' is the perfect Meredith delivery — casual, blunt, medical, slightly tragic. 'I ain't losing any more good parts' escalates it perfectly. This could ONLY be Meredith. High character integration score is warranted. Highly quotable, delivered deadpan.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'A week off, that'd be great.' (said as a positive response to the landlord saying the repairs would shut the office down for a week)
jokes.setup: The landlord presents 'shutting the office for a week' as a threat/burden
jokes.punchline: Stanley immediately and flatly welcomes it as great news
jokes.explanation: A classic Stanley beat — his hatred of work is one of the show's most reliable engines. The brevity and flatness make it work. Not original but perfectly executed.

jokes.text: Erin and Pete bickering about PowerPoint: 'You're the tutorial.' 'No, dude, I'm not. I'm not the tutorial.' 'You could be.' 'Mmm-mmm.'
jokes.setup: Pete doesn't want to teach Erin PowerPoint; she keeps pushing
jokes.punchline: 'You're the tutorial' — an oddly intimate and weird deflection that Erin seems to mean sincerely and Pete firmly rejects
jokes.explanation: Quirky and a little charming — this is establishing Erin and Pete's dynamic. 'You could be [the tutorial]' followed by Pete's firm 'Mmm-mmm' is a funny small exchange. The oddness of calling someone a tutorial has a very Erin quality.

jokes.text: Jim triumphantly reveals his sabotage: he microwaved a single kernel of popcorn in the office to trigger the EMF complaint. 'You popped one kernel.' 'Awesome, right?'
jokes.setup: Jim is shown secretly doing something in the office that we're meant to infer triggered the whole EMF complaint
jokes.punchline: It was one kernel of popcorn — a ridiculously minimal prank that somehow worked perfectly
jokes.explanation: Good reveal structure — the setup was laid in the previous scene with the landlord's visit. One kernel of popcorn setting off this whole chain of events is a satisfying payoff. Jim's conspiratorial delight is well-played. Works as both a prank reveal and a character moment about his devotion to Pam.

jokes.text: Kevin talking head: 'So Creed is that dude's stepdad?' Someone confirms. 'Well, I don't know about the rest of you, but I'm just going to say it. I'm nervous.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has apparently just learned something odd about Creed's family situation
jokes.punchline: Kevin airs his anxiety about this unsettling revelation with the earnest gravity of someone reporting a serious threat
jokes.explanation: Mild Creed gag — the implication that Creed being anyone's stepparent is alarming is well-founded. Kevin's 'I'm just going to say it' framing is funny. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'I'm sorry. I'm not growing a third arm. I know what Jim is trying to do...'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains he sees through Jim's scheme with the EMF scare
jokes.punchline: He calls Jim 'lucky Jimbo' and says he can 'live very happily in a magnetic field. Most of my childhood heroes got their powers that way.'
jokes.explanation: 'Most of my childhood heroes got their powers that way' is a perfect Dwight line — it reveals that he's both genre-savvy (he gets the superhero reference) and completely unironic about it. He's not using it as a deflection; he genuinely thinks magnetic field exposure might be beneficial. Excellent character integration. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight reading EMF side effects: 'Breast pain. No knobbies, no probbies. Nice try, Jim.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is reading through the list of EMF side effects to debunk them one by one
jokes.punchline: 'No knobbies, no probbies' — Dwight's invented rhyming slang for his flat chest as a defense against the breast pain warning
jokes.explanation: 'No knobbies, no probbies' is a genuinely inspired piece of Dwight-speak — it's rhyming, childish, specific, and totally in character. The casual dismissal of a medical symptom because he doesn't have breasts is absurdly logical in the best Dwight way. Very high quotability. Could only be Dwight.

jokes.text: Dwight reads 'Infertility' from the EMF side effects list, then the scene cuts to a beat of silence — implying he realizes this may explain his situation with Angela's baby
jokes.setup: Dwight has been smugly dismissing each EMF side effect; 'infertility' is the last one listed
jokes.punchline: The comedic pause — the audience understands before Dwight fully processes it — planting the seed of the episode's emotional B-plot
jokes.explanation: A masterful beat — the silence after 'Infertility' does all the work. The audience has context Dwight doesn't fully have yet. It's simultaneously funny (Dwight's smugness deflating) and genuinely affecting. Economy score is 9.0 because nothing needs to be said — the pause IS the joke AND the drama. This is the kind of layered moment The Office does better than almost anyone.

jokes.text: Pam asks Dwight to grab her popcorn. He refuses with 'Keep your snacks on your side, Jim, idiot.' The popcorn bag has mysteriously popped further — impossible on a new bag.
jokes.setup: Jim planted one kernel of popcorn to trigger the EMF scare; now on the work bus the evidence of microwave activity keeps appearing
jokes.punchline: More kernels have popped from a 'brand-new bag' — physically impossible, revealing more of Jim's prank infrastructure
jokes.explanation: Good escalating callback to Jim's prank. Dwight calling Pam 'Jim, idiot' (apparently a reflex) is a funny character beat. The impossible popcorn situation is a nice slow-burn visual gag.

jokes.text: Dwight's reaction of dawning horror to the impossible popcorn — 'Oh, my God.'
jokes.setup: Dwight insisted the EMF danger was fake and has been dismissing Jim's concerns all episode
jokes.punchline: Physical evidence appears to contradict him — the popcorn has clearly been microwaved by something — and Dwight's 'Oh, my God' suggests he's now terrified
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat works because of context — Dwight went from total denial to horror in a second. Works better on rewatch knowing the full prank. The 'Oh, my God' is understated but effective.

jokes.text: Jim's planned romantic gesture for Pam: 'I'm going to drive you up to the lake. Give you a whole week on the water, just you, me and the kids.' Pam: 'Can we stop by that pie stand on the way?'
jokes.setup: Jim has set up this elaborate prank to get Pam a week off — it's a grand romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: Pam's first response is not emotional gratitude but practical pie-related logistics
jokes.explanation: Charming deflation of a grand romantic moment with the mundane. Pam cutting straight to pie logistics while Jim is in romantic-gesture mode is a good domestically-grounded couple beat.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam negotiate the pie order: 'A dozen different pies? Because that means rhubarb.' 'Why would you say that? I meant four apple, four blueberry, two cherry, one peach, one chocolate. I thought that was implied.'
jokes.setup: Pam wants to stop at the pie stand; Jim says 'we'll get a dozen'
jokes.punchline: Jim has a very specific pie breakdown already worked out — 'I thought that was implied' — revealing he's thought about this pie trip in obsessive detail
jokes.explanation: The specificity is the joke — Jim's completely worked-out pie allocation delivered as if it's common knowledge. 'I thought that was implied' is the best line. The rhubarb anxiety from Pam gets paid off later, adding rewatch value.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals a loophole: his contract requires him to provide a 'temporary workspace.' He's ordered a work bus. Cut to: commercial for the Work Bus.
jokes.setup: Everyone is excited about a week off; Dwight announces a 'settlement'
jokes.punchline: Instead of time off, a rented work bus arrives — complete with a cheesy infomercial-style promo video
jokes.explanation: Great Dwight move — he found a contractual loophole to technically comply while completely defeating the purpose. The work bus infomercial ('Roll into the future with Work Bus') is a funny piece of corporate absurdism. 'In this age of belt-tightening and less empowered workers' is a great parodic detail.

jokes.text: Work Bus promo video: 'In this age of belt-tightening and less empowered workers, a work bus is how tomorrow gets things done.'
jokes.setup: The work bus promo is selling the concept of a mobile office
jokes.punchline: The promo casually acknowledges 'less empowered workers' as a selling point — workers too beaten down to demand actual offices
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical writing baked into the background. 'Less empowered workers' is a genuinely dark joke about the gig economy/cost-cutting dressed as a feature, not a bug. Smart but doesn't get a big reaction because it's subtle background material.

jokes.text: Someone gets on the work bus and it's comically crowded — person says 'Sorry. Oh, my God!' and someone yells 'Lose weight!'
jokes.setup: The staff is boarding the work bus, which is clearly very cramped
jokes.punchline: The overcrowding immediately produces a personal insult about body size
jokes.explanation: Weak joke — 'Lose weight!' is an unattributed cheap shot with no character specificity, no setup, and no twist. It's the most obvious possible response to a crowded bus gag. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: Nellie finds the adoption form; Andy says 'Oh, of course, you were adopted.' Nellie: 'I wish! No, I made some short lists, I had a couple of sleepovers, but I never managed to get in the end zone. I don't know what it was. Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.'
jokes.setup: Andy sees Nellie with adoption paperwork and assumes she was adopted
jokes.punchline: Nellie reveals she WASN'T adopted — she was a child who wanted to be adopted but wasn't chosen, delivered with breezy resignation. 'Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The premise — a child who went through the adoption process repeatedly but was never chosen — is inherently dark, but Nellie's delivery is cheerfully matter-of-fact: 'I had a couple of sleepovers, but I never managed to get in the end zone.' Using sports metaphors for failed adoption attempts is darkly brilliant. 'Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.' is perfectly calibrated — sad, funny, and deeply character-specific. Only Nellie.

jokes.text: Dwight's button on the adoption anecdote: 'Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just described being rejected from adoption as a child
jokes.punchline: His complete equanimity about this devastating self-assessment — 'Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.' — is the perfect Dwight response to personal tragedy
jokes.explanation: Five words that do extraordinary work. 'Not loveable, maybe. Oh, well.' is perfect economy — Dwight's self-awareness is almost there (he correctly identifies the likely problem) but his stoic acceptance of it is the twist. The 'Oh, well' dismissal is devastating comedy. This is among the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Nellie: '[Andy] hates me. Thinks I'm a monster. Should go back to Loch Ness.'
jokes.setup: Nellie is asking Oscar to help with the adoption form but doesn't want Andy to know
jokes.punchline: Her self-aware summary of Andy's view of her — 'Should go back to Loch Ness' — delivered completely deadpan
jokes.explanation: 'Should go back to Loch Ness' is a funny, specific, oddly poetic phrase. Nellie summarizing Andy's hatred with resigned acceptance and a monster metaphor is economical and characterful. The Scottish accent connection is a nice specific touch.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'How many times do you need to take a stroll?' Unnamed character: 'My legs cramp up, okay? It's a circulation issue.' Someone: 'Boy, I will hammerspank your rear.'
jokes.setup: Someone keeps getting up to pace in the cramped work bus
jokes.punchline: 'I will hammerspank your rear' — an absurdly specific and old-fashioned threat
jokes.explanation: 'Hammerspank' is a weird, invented compound verb that's funny in isolation. The scene establishes the work bus cramped-quarters chaos. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Someone spills a drink on Pam; Dwight smirks and tells Jim: 'And your woman drips with beverage.'
jokes.setup: Jim arranged the work bus to do something nice for Pam; instead Pam gets soaked
jokes.punchline: Dwight's arch, almost Shakespearean 'your woman drips with beverage' as he gloats
jokes.explanation: 'Your woman drips with beverage' is a perfectly ridiculous Dwight line — formal, archaic language applied to a mundane embarrassment. 'Drips with beverage' is just funny phrasing. The scene also contains 'locked in a prison bus' which is another good Dwight characterization. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dwight to Jim after Pam gets soaked: 'You forced me to spend money on needless repairs. And now you're locked in a prison bus and your woman drips with beverage.'
jokes.setup: Jim appeals to Dwight to help make the day better after his romantic plan backfires
jokes.punchline: Dwight's triumphant summary of Jim's failures — 'prison bus' for the work bus, 'drips with beverage' — culminating in refusing to spend money on gas
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the Dwight gloating beat. 'Prison bus' is a good characterization. Works as escalation of the prior joke. Slightly less impactful as a standalone since it repeats the 'drips with beverage' line.

jokes.text: Andy rallies the office to demand pie; the crowd chants 'Pies! Pies! Pies! Pies!' Andy responds: 'All right! The fat people have spoken!'
jokes.setup: Andy convinces the group they'd be more productive near the pie stand; Dwight resists
jokes.punchline: Andy's rallying cry and then immediately characterizing his victorious colleagues as 'the fat people'
jokes.explanation: 'The fat people have spoken' is a funny unexpected reframe — Andy immediately classifies his allies by their presumed pie appetite. It's blunt and oddly democratic. Medium-grade Andy character comedy.

jokes.text: Andy's capitulation: 'All right! The fat people have spoken!'
jokes.setup: Andy is pressured by the entire bus to go get pies
jokes.punchline: Andy frames his democratic capitulation as yielding to a specific demographic — 'the fat people' — which is both insulting and weirdly democratic
jokes.explanation: A mildly cheap joke that works mainly on Andy's clueless delivery. The body-targeting is lazy but the 'the fat people have spoken' framing — as though channeling the Voice of the People — has some comic architecture. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: Someone on the bus starts a 'Shabooya Roll Call' — a rhythmic call-and-response chant — and the whole bus joins in with personalized verses.
jokes.setup: The bus trip has turned into something resembling a fun road trip
jokes.punchline: The office breaks into an absurd, elaborate chant game with individual verses — Pam's verse ('I like to paint / You think you're better? / Oh no you ain't!') and Kevin's ('That is my name / They call me Kevin / 'Cause that's my name') are the highlights
jokes.explanation: A great set piece. Kevin's verse ('They call me Kevin / 'Cause that's my name') is perfect — it's the most Kevin possible response to being asked to characterize himself in a chant. Pam's defensive artist verse is also character-specific. The whole sequence works because everyone commits. High impact in a group viewing context.

jokes.text: Camera cut to someone taking a photo: 'Playing a little hookey from work today.' — ironic, since they're literally on a work bus
jokes.setup: The office is on the mandatory work bus
jokes.punchline: Someone frames it as playing hooky, which is technically impossible since they're on a work bus ordered by their employer — the self-deception is the joke
jokes.explanation: A minor observational beat. The irony lands softly — it's not sharp enough to be memorable but captures the office's collective self-delusion well.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Why isn't he scheming? Or preparing to avenge?' Pam: 'He's fine. He's indestructible.'
jokes.setup: Jim worries about Dwight's sulking
jokes.punchline: Jim's characterization of Dwight's normal state as 'scheming' or 'preparing to avenge' — and Pam's total confidence in his indestructibility
jokes.explanation: 'Preparing to avenge' as a description of Dwight's default mode is funny and accurate. Works well as character shorthand.

jokes.text: Oscar helping Nellie with adoption form: 'Always say that a child is placed for adoption, never surrendered. We're not hostages. Although, I have considered kidnapping one. And never say that.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is coaching Nellie on adoption terminology
jokes.punchline: Oscar's adoption coaching goes off the rails when he admits he has 'considered kidnapping one' — immediately followed by his own correction
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The setup is almost pedagogical — Oscar correcting adoption language — which makes the pivot to 'I have considered kidnapping one' completely unexpected. His immediate self-correction 'And never say that' is perfect economy. The joke works on structure alone. High quotability.

jokes.text: Oscar to Nellie: 'I wish I could just wave a magic wand and make you a parentless five-year-old again. I would snap you up.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is expressing enthusiasm for Nellie's adoption plans
jokes.punchline: He expresses this by wishing he could retroactively make Nellie an orphan so he could adopt her — a deeply weird and dark compliment delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and genuinely sweet at the same time. 'I wish I could make you a parentless five-year-old' is a startling thing to say, but Oscar means it as a compliment about Nellie's adoptability. The contrast between the dark premise and the warm intent is perfectly calibrated. Works especially well following Nellie's earlier admission that she was never adopted.

jokes.text: Kevin suddenly does mental math to calculate if they'll make it to the pie stand in time. 'At 55 miles an hour, that just gives us five minutes to spare!'
jokes.setup: Someone mentions the pie stand closes at 5:00 and they're 13 miles away
jokes.punchline: Kevin — who is known for being bad at math — instantly calculates the exact travel time in his head
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. Kevin's math incompetence is a long-running trait, so his sudden savant-level pie-math is the perfect inversion. It works because it's not just 'Kevin is good at math' — it's specifically that PIE unlocks his capacity. Sets up the follow-up beautifully.

jokes.text: Jim tests Kevin's math with '19,154 pies divided by 61 pies' — Kevin instantly says '314 pies.' Then Jim asks 'What if it were salads?' Kevin starts adding: 'Carry the four... In the... It doesn't work.'
jokes.setup: Kevin just did instant pie math; Jim wants to test if it's pie-specific
jokes.punchline: Kevin instantly answers the pie division problem but completely fails at the salad version — confirming his math ability is exclusively pie-activated
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the better Kevin jokes in the entire series. The structure is flawless: establish the ability, immediately test it, confirm the absurd limitation. 'What if it were salads?' and Kevin's collapse into 'It doesn't work' is perfectly calibrated. It's not just funny — it's a complete theory of Kevin's character. The specificity (19,154 divided by 61 = 314 is actually correct) shows the writers did the math. Could ONLY be Kevin. Approaches the anchor of legendary character-based TV comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals the bus is 'almost out of gas' and refuses to stop at a name-brand station because it's 'five cents a gallon extra. The tanks are so big on this thing, it really adds up.'
jokes.setup: The group is racing to the pie stand; Dwight announces they need gas
jokes.punchline: Dwight's penny-pinching is so extreme that he'd rather fail to reach the destination than pay the brand-name premium — framed as completely reasonable fiscal responsibility
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight — petty financial obstruction dressed as prudent management. 'It really adds up' delivered with total sincerity while people who want pie are begging him is good character work.

jokes.text: Jim leads the group in chanting 'What do we want? Pies! When do we want it? Pies!' — the group answers 'Pies' to both questions.
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to rally the group against Dwight's refusal to get gas at the nearby station
jokes.punchline: The protest chant where 'Pies' is both the demand AND the timeline — 'When do we want it? Pies!'
jokes.explanation: Classic protest chant subversion. 'When do we want it? Pies!' is a funny twist on the format — the group is too pie-focused to understand the chant structure. Mildly original.

jokes.text: Dwight concedes dramatically: 'You win, Jim! You win... You are the alpha male. There you go. Alpha male, go buy your wife a pie. Go buy the whole world a pie!' Jim: 'That's impossible.' Dwight: [drives away without them]
jokes.setup: Dwight appears to dramatically concede to Jim's demands
jokes.punchline: His concession speech escalates to the absurd ('Buy the whole world a pie!'), and when Jim correctly notes that's impossible, Dwight drives the bus away — leaving everyone stranded
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight move — the fake concession speech that's actually a setup for petty revenge. 'Buy the whole world a pie' as escalating sarcasm followed by Jim's literal response 'That's impossible' is a nice straight-man beat. Then Dwight actually driving away is the physical escalation that makes it land. Strong Dwight character work.

jokes.text: Phyllis, after Dwight drives away: 'Well, now I don't even feel like pie.' Beat. 'Wait. No, it's back.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has abandoned everyone at the gas station in a petty power move
jokes.punchline: Phyllis briefly loses her pie enthusiasm from the emotional whiplash — then it immediately returns
jokes.explanation: Deceptively simple and extremely funny. 'Wait. No, it's back.' is a three-word punchline that's perfectly timed and delivered. The joke is about how fleeting the emotional effect of abandonment is when pie is at stake. Pure economy. The beat between 'I don't even feel like pie' and 'Wait. No, it's back.' is the joke. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Phyllis, urgently: 'They're going to be out of banana cream. Banana cream is the first to go. We'll be lucky to get pumpkin at this point.'
jokes.setup: The group is stranded and someone urges Jim to go check on Dwight
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's framing of the banana cream situation as a genuine crisis with escalating pie triage
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the pie anxiety. 'We'll be lucky to get pumpkin at this point' as a downgraded expectation is funny. The pie triage logic tracks perfectly.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional (on the roof of the bus): 'My trouser hives are void of honey. I had congress with Angela, and the child that she bore did not issue from my loins. I thought I would be a father and instead I am a eunuch, neutered by my own building.'
jokes.setup: Jim confronts Dwight and asks why he's being difficult; Dwight reveals the real issue
jokes.punchline: Dwight's revelation of infertility is delivered in his most formal, archaic register: 'trouser hives void of honey,' 'had congress with Angela,' 'did not issue from my loins' — grief expressed through Dwight's unique vocabulary
jokes.explanation: The episode's most complex and best-written moment. Dwight's vocabulary here is extraordinary: 'trouser hives are void of honey' for infertility is absurd, poetic, and completely specific to Dwight's beekeeping-inflected worldview. 'Neutered by my own building' is darkly funny and also genuinely sad. 'Had congress with Angela' as a formal euphemism is perfect. This is what great character comedy looks like — the humor and the pathos are inseparable. Approaches the calibration anchor for 9+ territory.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Is this about the popcorn, or the X on the ceiling?' Dwight: 'Dwight, that was a prank.' Jim: 'That's genius. That's the best prank you've ever done.'
jokes.setup: Jim confesses his popcorn prank to Dwight to console him
jokes.punchline: Dwight — having just been devastated — immediately pivots to admiring Jim's prank as the best one ever done, with genuine respect
jokes.explanation: Dwight pivoting from grief to admiring Jim's prank is a perfect character beat — Dwight's appreciation for good pranksmanship overrides his devastation, and he can't help but give credit where credit is due. The emotional whiplash is very Dwight. 'You'll take it' is a good closer.

jokes.text: Andy reads Nellie's letter and declares it 'unsignable' — 'It's inaccurate, dishonest, and in a word, dong water.'
jokes.setup: Nellie wrote her own character reference and asked Andy to sign it
jokes.punchline: 'In a word, dong water' — Andy's invented insult for terrible quality documents
jokes.explanation: 'Dong water' as a one-word summary is a perfect Andy insult — juvenile, invented, strangely vivid, and delivered with the gravitas of a legal term. Very quotable. Only Andy would use this phrase while reading on a rooftop.

jokes.text: Andy dismisses Nellie: 'You asked me to do you a favor. I did it. I read it. Thank you very much to me for my time. Good luck with your impossible dream.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just rejected Nellie's letter as unsignable
jokes.punchline: 'Thank you very much to me for my time' — Andy congratulating himself for doing a bad job of someone else's favor
jokes.explanation: 'Thank you very much to me for my time' and 'Good luck with your impossible dream' are both terrific Andy lines. The self-congratulation for a non-favor is perfectly Andy. 'Impossible dream' adopts the grandiosity while being cruel — pure character.

jokes.text: Dwight asks Jim how long it took him and Pam to conceive. Jim refuses to say. Dwight: 'What position did you use to conceive? Regular or lady-on-her-back? You used lady-on-her-back, didn't you, freak? Yuck, gross. Never mind, Jim.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to console Dwight about his infertility by saying couples sometimes take years
jokes.punchline: Dwight's rapid-fire interrogation about conception positions, escalating to self-disgust at the thought of Jim's sex life
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight. His clinical-then-grossed-out pivot is perfectly timed. 'Lady-on-her-back' as his clinical euphemism is funny. His calling Jim a 'freak' for presumably using the most conventional position, then immediately regretting the thought ('Yuck, gross. Never mind') is great — Dwight's curiosity outrunning his disgust. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight, about Nellie crying on the bus: 'British women, famously over-emotional, am I right?'
jokes.setup: Nellie has burst into tears on the bus — presumably having overheard Andy's rejection
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response is a fake-casual cultural generalization delivered to fill the awkward silence
jokes.explanation: Dwight filling an emotional moment with a completely wrong-headed generalization is characteristically oblivious. Works as awkward silence deflection. The specificity of 'British women, famously over-emotional' (the opposite of the stereotype) is the joke.

jokes.text: Jim suggests to Dwight that because he owns the building, 'everyone in it, we're all kind of like your children.' Dwight reveals: 'You know there's a phrase about that in German, bildenkinder, used almost exclusively by childless landlords to console themselves.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to reframe Dwight's childlessness by suggesting his tenants are his 'children'
jokes.punchline: Dwight not only knows an obscure German word for this but adds the devastating contextual detail that it's 'used almost exclusively by childless landlords to console themselves' — meaning people have been making this exact pity-argument to Dwight-types for centuries
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The construction is brilliant: Jim makes a sincere, nice attempt at comfort, and Dwight's knowledge of an obscure German consolation phrase specifically designed for this situation undercuts the comfort entirely — the phrase's existence proves people have been patronizing childless landlords for so long they invented a word for it. The specificity ('almost exclusively by childless landlords') is devastating. Could only be Dwight. Strong candidate for the episode's best written joke.

jokes.text: Jim, trying to use Dwight's own 'bildenkinder' against him: 'Now you have a bus full of real bildenkinder.' Dwight: 'Bildenkinder. Okay, and they're all dangerously close to not getting pie. And there's only one guy who can save them.' Jim: 'It's not me.' Dwight: 'I agree. Oh.'
jokes.setup: Jim uses Dwight's German word to appeal to his paternal instincts
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response pivots from accepting the framing to revealing that Jim said 'It's not me' — before Dwight even implied Jim wasn't the one — which means Jim knows it has to be Dwight
jokes.explanation: Good tight dialogue exchange. The rhythm of Jim pre-emptively disqualifying himself and Dwight's 'I agree. Oh.' — the 'Oh' being the moment Dwight realizes he's been maneuvered — is well-structured. Jim working Dwight through his own framework is satisfying.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight's exchange: 'And they're all dangerously close to not getting pie. And there's only one guy who can save them.' Dwight: 'It's not me.' Jim: 'I agree.' Dwight: 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Jim is framing the pie mission as a heroic narrative to motivate Dwight
jokes.punchline: Dwight pre-emptively declines the hero role ('It's not me.'); Jim's immediate agreement ('I agree.') deflates Dwight rather than inspiring him. Dwight's 'Oh.' registers the surprise of not being argued with.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure here — setup, unexpected agreement, deflated 'Oh.' — is elegantly brief. Dwight has set himself up to be argued into heroism and Jim refuses to play along, which is almost crueler. The 'Oh.' is perfect.

jokes.text: Dwight drives the bus at full speed toward the pie stand — Jim and Pam scramble. Pam says rhubarb is actually the one pie she doesn't like; Jim cuts her off: 'Don't.' She says it again. 'Don't.' 'Everybody, hang on!'
jokes.setup: Jim promised Pam a rhubarb pie specifically; Pam tries to clarify she doesn't actually like rhubarb
jokes.punchline: Jim refuses to hear this information — twice — because it would undermine his romantic gesture; Dwight's dangerous driving renders the conversation moot
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the earlier rhubarb setup. Jim's 'Don't' said twice — refusing to let Pam ruin his gesture by having the wrong pie preference — is a funny, relatable bit. The callback to the specific pie breakdown from earlier makes it more satisfying. Dwight's sudden reckless driving is a physical escalation that interrupts the scene perfectly.

jokes.text: The office erupts: 'Pie! Pie! Pie! Pie!' as they arrive at Laverne's
jokes.setup: The pie mission reaches its destination
jokes.punchline: The collective 'Pie! Pie! Pie!' chant — callback to the earlier chant — signals the absurd triumph of office workers who just need something simple to be happy
jokes.explanation: The payoff chant works because the episode has earned it — we've spent 20 minutes caring about these people getting pie. The emotional satisfaction amplifies the comedy. Not a sophisticated joke, but effective.

jokes.text: Andy has signed Nellie's letter — with modifications. He reads his addendum: 'She's tough in business, but tender with the people she cares about. She'll make a wonderful mother to any child who can overlook weird accents.'
jokes.setup: Andy refused to sign Nellie's letter; now he appears to have had a change of heart
jokes.punchline: His sincere endorsement is undercut by the final clause: 'who can overlook weird accents' — a genuine attempt at a compliment that accidentally reveals his lingering contempt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. The setup is an emotional beat — Andy's unexpected kindness — and the punchline undercuts it perfectly without entirely destroying the warmth. 'Who can overlook weird accents' is exactly what Andy would add, and it works both as a joke and as character development. The line is technically still an endorsement, which is why it's better than a pure insult. Highly quotable, beautifully structured.

jokes.text: Kevin approaches Oscar with a pie. Oscar realizes Kevin wants to get hit in the face with a pie and says so. Kevin: 'You don't have the guts, you stupid, dumb do-do face.'
jokes.setup: The group has pie; Kevin has engineered a scenario where Oscar will pie him
jokes.punchline: Kevin's escalating trash talk to provoke Oscar: 'stupid, dumb do-do face' — the most childish possible insult for the purpose of getting pie in the face
jokes.explanation: 'Stupid, dumb do-do face' is a perfectly Kevin insult — he's not trying to actually wound Oscar, he just needs to provoke him enough to get a pie thrown. The childishness of the language in service of the goal is very Kevin. The scene plays great as physical comedy payoff.

jokes.text: Oscar pies Kevin in the face. Kevin's response: 'Yes!' Then: 'Oh, my God, I'm getting so stuffed.'
jokes.setup: Kevin engineered getting a pie thrown at him
jokes.punchline: His triumphant 'Yes!' at being hit with pie, followed by eating it off his face: 'Oh, my God, I'm getting so stuffed.'
jokes.explanation: 'I'm getting so stuffed' after being hit with a pie is a perfect Kevin character beat — he's eating pie off his face and it's delightful. The 'Yes!' of triumph at achieving his goal is a great physical comedy button. Kevin's relationship with food as primary motivation runs through the whole episode and this is its logical conclusion.

jokes.text: Dwight and Jim moment: 'We did it.' 'You did it.'
jokes.setup: The pie mission has been accomplished; Jim and Dwight have a quiet moment
jokes.punchline: Jim says 'We did it' but Dwight corrects to 'You did it' — refusing to share credit while also implicitly acknowledging Jim's success
jokes.explanation: A small warm moment played as a slight joke. 'You did it' — Dwight refusing collaborative credit — is characteristic. Works better as an emotional beat than a pure joke, but the delivery has a comedic edge.

jokes.text: Andy joins the Shabooya Roll Call on the bus: 'My name is Andy / I don't do drugs / Now check the style / Of Flatt and Scruggs!'
jokes.setup: The Shabooya Roll Call has been going around the bus; it's Andy's turn
jokes.punchline: Andy's verse is a random, inexplicable reference to bluegrass musicians Flatt and Scruggs — completely off-brand for the chant and deeply Andy
jokes.explanation: The Flatt and Scruggs reference as Andy's self-defining chant verse is perfectly Andy — preppy, tries-too-hard, niche musical knowledge deployed at the wrong moment. 'Now check the style of Flatt and Scruggs' in a hip-hop-influenced chant is a great tonal collision. The self-declaration 'I don't do drugs' as his defining characteristic is funny in its specificity and randomness.

jokes.text: Final beat: Someone says 'What?' — the implicit reaction to Andy's Flatt and Scruggs verse
jokes.setup: Andy has just declared 'Now check the style of Flatt and Scruggs'
jokes.punchline: Someone's confused 'What?' as the final button on the episode
jokes.explanation: A clean button — the 'What?' is exactly the right response to Andy's verse and closes the episode with the right comic note. Simple but well-placed.

tmdb_overview: The staffers hit the road in a rented bus when the building is deemed unsafe. Meanwhile, Nellie reaches out to Andy for help in adopting a baby, and Jim uses pie to spread cheer to Pam.
